name: LookRank
subcategory: AI face rating and looksmaxxing feedback
tagline: Upload selfies and get an AI attractiveness score with ranked breakdowns and improvement tips.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Strip away the progress rings and this is one vision-model call with a strict rubric and a JSON response. An agent can wire a local page that takes three photos, asks a multimodal model for subscores on symmetry, skin, jawline, hair and grooming, and returns blunt, actionable notes. The one thing you cannot honestly rebuild is the percentile: ranking you against a population needs a population, and nobody outside the app knows how that number is actually computed. That is less of a loss than it sounds, because the ranking in apps like this is a presentation layer on the same model vibes you can get yourself. Build it, keep the photos on your own disk, and skip the part where a subscription tells you your face is a 6.2 out of 10.
coreLoopDIY: Drop in a few photos, get rubric-based subscores, an overall number and a short list of things worth changing, stored locally.
requirements: An API key for a multimodal model (OpenAI, Anthropic or Google)
Willingness to send your own face to a model API
whatYouLose: Percentile ranking against a large user base, which no local build can fake honestly
Score stability over time: models drift and re-runs will wobble unless you pin the model and cache results
A polished mobile app with camera guidance, lighting hints and before/after tracking
Curated routines and product recommendations bolted onto each weak subscore
Any pretense of clinical or aesthetic-professional grounding
moatNotes: The dataset of scored faces is the only real asset, and it mostly powers a percentile that users treat as gospel.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the number is the product, and a number that comes from an app with a million users feels more authoritative than the same number from a script you wrote yesterday. The onboarding, the camera prompts, the progress tracking over months and the tidy routine attached to each weak area are all friction the local build skips. There is also the obvious thing: most people do not want to set up an API key and paste photo paths into a terminal to find out how they look, and the app is priced squarely at that reluctance.
notes: A rubric, a vision model and a bar chart will get you most of the way. The remainder is the percentile, which is the only part that needs other people's faces.
prompt:
Build a local-only web app called "Mirror" that scores face photos against a fixed rubric using a multimodal LLM.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. One route handler for the API call.
- No database. History goes in localStorage. Photos never leave the machine except in the single model request.
- Model: OpenAI gpt-4o via the official SDK, key read from process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY in .env.local. Ship .env.example.

Core flow:
1. Single page. Drag-and-drop or file-pick up to three images (front, three-quarter, profile). Show thumbnails, allow removal. Resize client-side to max 1024px and convert to base64 before sending.
2. POST the images to /api/score. The route sends one request with a system prompt that defines a strict rubric and demands JSON only, temperature 0, response_format json_object.
3. Rubric subscores, 0 to 10 with one decimal each: facial symmetry, skin quality, jawline and lower third, eye area, hair and hairline, grooming and styling, photo quality. Plus an overall score as a weighted average computed in code, not by the model, so the math is reproducible.
4. For each subscore the model returns one sentence of evidence and one concrete, cheap action. Instruct it to be specific and unsentimental, to refuse cosmetic surgery advice, and to say "insufficient photo quality" instead of guessing when an angle is missing.
5. Render results as a horizontal bar chart plus a table of actions sorted by expected impact. Show the exact rubric weights on screen.
6. Save each run to localStorage with date, scores and thumbnails. A history view shows subscore trends over time. Export and import the history as JSON. A clear-all button that actually clears.

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, payments, cloud storage, telemetry, any percentile or "you rank above X percent" claim, age or ethnicity inference, mobile app.

Honesty requirements: a short permanent banner stating the scores come from one language model and are not calibrated against any population. Refuse to process images that do not contain a face and say so plainly.

Deliver a README with setup in four commands, the rubric weights, and a note that re-running on the same photos can shift scores by a few tenths.
